title: Al-Baqarah: The Cow
intro: 26 days through Al-Baqarah, the longest surah of the Quran, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: Al-Baqarah, "The Cow", is the second and longest surah of the Quran: 286 verses, revealed in Medina after the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ moved there. After the letters Alif, Lam, Mim, it opens by presenting the Quran itself: a book beyond doubt, given as guidance. Commentators explain that it guides "those who ward off (evil)", the muttaqin, people of taqwa or mindful awareness of Allah, because they are the ones ready to benefit from it.

After describing believers, disbelievers and hypocrites, the surah turns to address everyone at once: "O mankind!" It is the first time the Quran, in its written order, calls out to all of humanity this way. The verse makes its most basic argument: the One who created you and those before you is the One to worship. The goal it names is taqwa, mindful awareness of Allah.

The verse asks those who reject faith a pointed question: how can they deny the One who gave them life? Its answer traces a whole existence in one line. Commentators such as Ibn Kathir explain "ye were dead" as the time before a person existed; then come life, death, life again at the resurrection, and finally the return to Allah. Every stage, the verse says, is in His hands.

Allah has told the angels He will place a khalifah, a vicegerent, on earth. He then teaches the Prophet Adam "all the names", which commentators understand as the names of things, and asks the angels to name them. This is their humble reply. Some Muslims recite it before studying, as a reminder of where knowledge comes from.

Allah commands the angels to bow before Adam, a prostration that classical commentators describe as one of honour, not worship. All obey except Iblis, who refuses out of pride; "demurred" here means refused. Commentators draw the lesson that arrogance, setting oneself above a command of Allah, lies at the root of his fall. Elsewhere the Quran says he was one of the jinn, and two verses later it calls him Satan.

After Adam and his wife eat from the forbidden tree, Adam receives "words" from his Lord, repents, and is forgiven. Many commentators identify these words with the prayer in Al-A'raf 7:23: "Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves." In Islamic teaching the slip is forgiven, and it is not passed on to Adam's children.

This is the story that gives the surah its name. The Prophet Musa (Moses) tells his people to sacrifice a cow, and instead of simply doing it they answer with questions: what age, what colour, what kind. Each answer narrows the task, until "they sacrificed her, though almost they did not." Commentators read it as a lesson about meeting a clear command with excuses: the more they stalled, the harder it became.

Two pillars of Islam appear together here: "worship", Pickthall's word for salah, the ritual prayer, and "the poor-due", zakat, the obligatory alms. The point is that no good deed is wasted: whatever good a person does is sent ahead and will be found waiting with Allah. The verse comes just after the believers are told to forgive and be patient in the face of hostility.

The point is that Allah is not confined to any place: East and West alike belong to Him, and He can be turned to from anywhere. Some classical commentators link the verse to voluntary prayer while travelling, or praying when the direction is unclear, as well as to the later change of the qiblah, the direction of prayer. "Countenance" translates wajh, literally "face", and "All-Embracing" is al-Wasi'.

The point is the ease of Allah's creative power: the heavens and the earth are His work, and whatever He decrees needs only His command. "Be! and it is" renders kun fa-yakun, a phrase that returns several times in the Quran. "Originator" translates Badi', one who brings something into being with no earlier model.

The surah turns to the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham), presented as the model of faith. Told to surrender, he answers at once: "I have surrendered to the Lord of the Worlds." The point is that this wholehearted submission is what the Quran means by islam; aslim and aslamtu come from the same root as Islam and Muslim. The next verse has him pass it on to his sons, as did the Prophet Ya'qub (Jacob).

This verse sits in the passage about the change of qiblah, the direction of prayer, from Jerusalem to the Kaaba in Mecca, early in the Medinan years. Rather than dwell on directions, it points to what matters: racing one another in good deeds. The Arabic, fastabiqu al-khayrat, is often quoted on its own.

One of the Quran's most intimate promises: remember Allah, and He will remember you. Remembrance, dhikr, covers prayer, recitation and the simple repetition of Allah's names and praises. Pickthall's "reject not Me" renders a word that also means "do not be ungrateful to Me".

This verse opens a short passage about trials and loss, and it begins by naming where help is found: in sabr and in prayer. Sabr, translated here as "steadfastness", means patient endurance: holding firm in difficulty, keeping up good deeds, and holding back from wrong. The verse ends with the reason these help: "Allah is with the steadfast."

The verse before warns of trials: fear, hunger, and loss of wealth, lives and crops, with good news for the steadfast. This verse gives their response, inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. Commentators explain its comfort: whatever is lost already belonged to Allah, and everyone is returning to Him. Muslims say it on hearing of a death and in moments of loss, large or small.

A one-line statement of tawhid, the oneness of Allah, the foundation of Islamic belief. It ends with the same two names of mercy that open the Bismillah. The next verse points to the evidence in creation: the heavens and the earth, night and day, ships, rain, winds and clouds.

This comes in the passage on the Hajj pilgrimage: after the rites, some ask only for good in this world, while others ask for good in both. According to a hadith reported by Anas ibn Malik, this was the supplication the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ made most often. It remains one of the best-known prayers in Islam.

In the middle of a long passage on marriage and divorce, the surah pauses to command care over the prayers. Commentators have seen a point in that placement: even amid the strains of divorce, and even in danger, as the next verse adds, prayer is not to be neglected. Scholars have long differed over "the midmost prayer": many hold that it is the afternoon prayer, Asr, while others name a different one.

posts.display: Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him. Unto Him belongeth whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is in the earth.
posts.display_original: ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلْحَىُّ ٱلْقَيُّومُ لَا تَأْخُذُهُۥ سِنَةٌ وَلَا نَوْمٌ لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ
posts.caption: The opening of Ayat al-Kursi, the Verse of the Throne, too long to show in full. It is a portrait of Allah as al-Hayy al-Qayyum, "the Alive, the Eternal": ever-living, sustaining all things, never touched by drowsiness or sleep, owner of all that is in the heavens and the earth. In a hadith recorded in Sahih Muslim it is called the greatest verse in the Book of Allah. Many Muslims recite the whole verse after prayers and before sleep.

Right after Ayat al-Kursi comes one of the Quran's most quoted lines. Classical commentators such as Ibn Kathir explain that since the truth has been made clear, there is no need to force anyone into faith. "False deities" renders taghut, anything worshipped in place of Allah, and the "firm handhold" is al-urwa al-wuthqa.

The surah's long passage on charity opens with this image, and its point is that giving for Allah's sake is never a loss: it grows. One grain sprouts seven ears with a hundred grains in each, seven hundred from one, and Allah multiplies it further still for whom He wills. "In Allah's way" renders fi sabil Allah.

The verses around this one warn against spoiling charity by reminding people of it or hurting their feelings. A kind word and forgiveness, it says, are worth more than a gift that wounds. "Absolute" renders al-Ghani, the One free of all need, and "Clement" al-Halim, the Forbearing.

In the passage on charity, the verse before contrasts Satan, who threatens people with poverty so they hold back, with Allah, who promises forgiveness and bounty. This verse names a gift worth more than wealth: hikmah, wisdom. Whoever is given it has received "abundant good", though only "men of understanding", ulu al-albab, people of insight, take the reminder to heart.

Al-Baqarah forbids riba, usury, in the verses just before this one. Then it turns to the borrower who cannot pay: the verse grants time until things ease, and calls cancelling the debt as charity better still. It is a window onto the Quran's concern for people in financial hardship.

Set among laws on trade and debt, this verse lifts the eye to what stands behind them: a day when everyone returns to Allah and every soul is repaid in full, with no one wronged. Even business, the point is, is done in view of that day. Early authorities named different verses as the last to be revealed; Ibn Abbas is reported to have said it was this one.

posts.display: Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope. For it (is only) that which it hath earned, and against it (only) that which it hath deserved. Our Lord! Condemn us not if we forget, or miss the mark!
posts.display_original: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتْ وَعَلَيْهَا مَا ٱكْتَسَبَتْ رَبَّنَا لَا تُؤَاخِذْنَآ إِن نَّسِينَآ أَوْ أَخْطَأْنَا
posts.caption: The final verse of Al-Baqarah, shown in part. It opens with the promise that no soul is burdened beyond its capacity, then becomes a prayer for pardon, mercy and help. According to a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, the last two verses of this surah are enough for whoever recites them at night. Thank you for reading Al-Baqarah with us.
